phishing.title: How Credential Phishing Works
phishing.why_it_works: Attackers create convincing replicas of trusted websites to trick you into entering your username and password. They exploit trust, urgency, and fear to bypass your critical thinking.
how_to_spot: Check the URL carefully - look for misspellings or extra characters in the domain
Legitimate services rarely ask you to verify credentials via email links
Look for HTTPS and verify the certificate matches the expected organization
Hover over links before clicking to see the actual destination
Watch for generic greetings like 'Dear Customer' instead of your name
phishing.content: Phishing is the most common cyber attack vector, responsible for over 80% of reported security incidents.

quiz.question: You receive an email from 'support@g00gle.com' asking you to verify your password. What should you do?
options: Click the link and enter your password to verify
Reply to the email asking if it is legitimate
Ignore the email and navigate directly to google.com to check your account
Forward it to all your contacts as a warning
quiz.explanation: Never click links in suspicious emails. Always navigate directly to the official website by typing the URL yourself.

credential_harvesting.title: How Credential Harvesting Works
credential_harvesting.why_it_works: Attackers set up fake login pages that look identical to real ones. When you enter your credentials, they capture them instantly and gain access to your real account.
how_to_spot: The URL domain does not match the service you expect
The page asks for more information than usual (e.g., SSN, bank details)
The SSL certificate does not match the organization
After submitting, you are redirected to the real site (to avoid suspicion)
credential_harvesting.content: Credential harvesting is a targeted form of phishing focused specifically on stealing login credentials.

quiz.question: A website asks for your bank login AND your ATM PIN. Is this normal?
options: Yes, banks always need both for verification
No, legitimate banks never ask for your ATM PIN online
Only if the URL starts with HTTPS
Yes, if the email looks official
quiz.explanation: Banks never ask for ATM PINs online. This is a clear sign of credential harvesting.

url_phishing.title: Recognizing Malicious URLs
url_phishing.why_it_works: Attackers use deceptive URLs that mimic legitimate websites. They exploit the fact that most people don't carefully examine URLs before clicking.
how_to_spot: Look for misspelled brand names (e.g., 'paypa1.com' instead of 'paypal.com')
Be wary of URLs with IP addresses instead of domain names
Check for suspicious top-level domains (.xyz, .tk, .click)
Watch for excessive subdomains (e.g., 'login.verify.account.evil.com')
url_phishing.content: URL phishing accounts for the majority of cyber fraud attempts.

quiz.question: Which URL is most likely a phishing attempt?
options: https://www.paypal.com/login
http://paypal-verify.account-security.xyz/login
https://www.paypal.com/us/signin
https://paypal.com
quiz.explanation: The URL 'paypal-verify.account-security.xyz' uses a suspicious domain (.xyz) and mimics PayPal's branding. Always check the actual domain name.

financial_fraud.title: Financial Fraud & Payment Scams
financial_fraud.why_it_works: Scammers create urgency around financial transactions, claiming refunds, prizes, or payment failures to trick you into transferring money or sharing banking credentials.
how_to_spot: Unexpected refund or prize notifications
Requests to share UPI PIN, OTP, or banking passwords
Pressure to act immediately on financial matters
Unknown payment requests from unfamiliar sources
financial_fraud.content: Financial fraud causes billions in losses annually. Never share banking credentials or OTPs with anyone.

quiz.question: A caller from 'your bank' asks for your OTP to process a refund. What should you do?
options: Share the OTP since they are from the bank
Ask them to call back later
Hang up and call the bank's official number to verify
Share only part of the OTP
quiz.explanation: Banks never ask for OTPs over the phone. Hang up and call the official bank number to verify any claims.

social_engineering.title: Social Engineering Tactics
social_engineering.why_it_works: Attackers manipulate human psychology using urgency, authority, fear, and curiosity to bypass your rational thinking and make you act impulsively.
how_to_spot: Messages creating extreme urgency ('Your account will be deleted in 24 hours')
Claims of authority ('This is from the CEO', 'IT Department requires...')
Emotional manipulation through fear or excitement
Requests that bypass normal procedures
social_engineering.content: Social engineering exploits human psychology rather than technical vulnerabilities.

quiz.question: An email from 'the CEO' urgently requests a wire transfer before end of day. What's the best action?
options: Process it immediately since it's from the CEO
Verify the request through a separate channel (phone call, in-person)
Reply to the email asking for confirmation
Forward it to your team to handle
quiz.explanation: Always verify urgent financial requests through a separate channel. CEO fraud (BEC) is one of the costliest cyber attacks.

malware.title: Malware & Malicious Attachments
malware.why_it_works: Malware disguises itself as legitimate files or software. Once executed, it can steal data, encrypt files for ransom, or give attackers remote access to your system.
how_to_spot: Unexpected email attachments, especially .exe, .bat, .js, .vbs files
Documents requesting you to 'enable macros' or 'enable content'
Files from unknown senders or unexpected sources
Double file extensions (e.g., 'document.pdf.exe')
malware.content: Never open attachments from unknown sources. Malware can compromise your entire system.

quiz.question: You receive a Word document that asks you to 'Enable Macros' to view content. What should you do?
options: Enable macros - it's just a Word document
Do NOT enable macros - this is a common malware delivery technique
Save the file and scan it later
Forward it to a colleague to check
quiz.explanation: Macro-enabled documents are one of the most common malware delivery methods. Never enable macros in documents from untrusted sources.

impersonation.title: Brand & Authority Impersonation
impersonation.why_it_works: Attackers impersonate trusted brands, government agencies, or authority figures to exploit the trust you have in these entities.
how_to_spot: Check sender email domains carefully (e.g., 'support@amaz0n-help.com' vs 'support@amazon.com')
Official organizations rarely contact you via SMS with links
Government agencies don't request personal info via email
Look for poor grammar or generic templates
impersonation.content: Impersonation attacks are highly effective because they exploit pre-existing trust relationships.

quiz.question: An SMS from 'HDFC Bank' asks you to update KYC via a link. The sender ID shows 'HDFCBNK'. Is it safe?
options: Yes, the sender ID matches HDFC
No, sender IDs can be spoofed. Visit the bank branch or official app instead
Safe if the link starts with HTTPS
Safe if I don't enter my password
quiz.explanation: SMS sender IDs can be easily spoofed. Always use official bank apps or visit a branch for KYC updates.

unknown.title: General Cybersecurity Awareness
unknown.why_it_works: Cyber threats constantly evolve. Understanding basic security principles helps you recognize and avoid new attack types as they emerge.
how_to_spot: Any unsolicited communication requesting personal information
Offers that seem too good to be true
Pressure to act quickly without time to think
Requests to bypass standard security procedures
unknown.content: Stay vigilant and always verify before you trust.

quiz.question: What is the single most important thing you can do to protect your online accounts?
options: Use the same strong password everywhere
Use unique passwords and enable two-factor authentication
Only use websites that look professional
Never use public WiFi
quiz.explanation: Using unique passwords with two-factor authentication is the most effective protection against account compromise.

general_security.title: Basic Security Hygiene
general_security.why_it_works: Many attacks succeed because of poor security habits. Strong fundamentals protect against the majority of common threats.
how_to_spot: Keep all software and operating systems updated
Use unique, strong passwords for every account
Enable two-factor authentication wherever possible
Be skeptical of unsolicited communications
general_security.content: Good security hygiene prevents most common attacks.

quiz.question: Why is reusing passwords across multiple accounts dangerous?
options: It makes passwords harder to remember
If one account is breached, all accounts using that password are compromised
It slows down your computer
It violates terms of service
quiz.explanation: Password reuse means one breach can cascade across all your accounts. Always use unique passwords.
